channel.description: An automatically generated daily podcast for the serious gardener and designer. Most episodes end with a short spaced-repetition quiz on plants covered earlier, to build lasting recall.

item.title: The Daily Plant — Culver's Root (Veronicastrum virginicum)
item.description:
Midsummer means Veronicastrum virginicum: the candelabra-spiked native perennial that bridges late June through August with genuine vertical structure. This episode covers its prairie-leaning native range and what that means for East Coast specification, its demanding establishment timeline, its exceptional pollinator credentials including ties to the endangered rusty-patched bumblebee, and the cultivar choices — 'Lavender Towers', 'Fascination', 'Album' — worth knowing. Followed by spaced-repetition recall on Lindera benzoin, Persicaria, Agastache, and Helianthus.

item.title: The Daily Plant — Native Sunflowers (Helianthus)
item.description:
An expert-level genus deep dive on Helianthus, the native perennial sunflowers of the East Coast. The episode covers the five perennial species an East Coast designer needs to know — swamp sunflower, woodland sunflower, thinleaf sunflower, Appalachian sunflower, and Jerusalem artichoke (and why to never specify the last one) — along with a provenance warning about the Midwestern species sold as East Coast natives. Closes with the genus's ecological story: oligolectic specialist bees in Andrena and Melissodes, butterfly host-plant relationships with the Silvery Checkerspot, and late-season seed value for birds.

item.description:

item.title: The Daily Plant — Persicaria: From Garden Star to Invasive Vine
item.description:
The genus Persicaria — currently in taxonomic flux as part of it migrates toward the genus Bistorta — spans some of the best long-season perennials available for a midsummer-through-frost mid-border all the way to one of the most aggressive invasive vines spreading through East Coast natural areas. This episode covers the ornamental species and cultivars designers should be specifying, the native East Coast species worth knowing, the weedy annual found in every disturbed-soil site, mile-a-minute weed and how to manage it, and the critical distinction from Japanese knotweed.

item.title: The Daily Plant — Ninebark (Physocarpus opulifolius)
item.description:
Physocarpus opulifolius — ninebark — is one of the most site-tolerant native shrubs in the East Coast palette, yet it's often under-specified in its most ecologically valuable forms while its showier cultivars take center stage. This episode covers the plant's genuine cultural adaptability, the powdery mildew data that should drive cultivar selection, the critical nativar trade-off between foliage color and wildlife value, and a practical cultivar shortlist for designers. Followed by spaced-repetition review of Oxydendrum arboreum, Cephalanthus occidentalis, and Solidago.

item.title: The Daily Plant — Goldenrod (Solidago)
item.description:
Today's episode dives into Solidago, the goldenrod genus — a keystone group of East Coast natives that supports over a hundred butterfly and moth species, roughly fifteen specialist bee species, and a cascade of wildlife relationships no other late-summer genus can match. We work through the garden-worthy species, from Solidago rugosa 'Fireworks' to the shade-tolerant Solidago caesia to the clump-forming Solidago speciosa, and tackle the cultivar question with findings from the Mount Cuba Center's three-year, seventy-plant trial. The episode closes with a spaced-repetition quiz covering Phlox, Schizachyrium scoparium, Agastache, and Nyssa sylvatica.

item.title: The Daily Plant — Black Gum (Nyssa sylvatica)
item.description:
Nyssa sylvatica — black gum, black tupelo, pepperidge — is one of the East Coast's finest native canopy trees and one of the most underspecified. This episode covers the full designer's brief: the critical taproot transplanting constraint you cannot ignore, the exceptional moisture tolerance from summer drought to seasonally flooded sites, how to navigate cultivar selection for reliable fall color, and the tree's substantial ecological role from spring nectar bloom through fall fruit as a songbird migration fuel stop.

item.title: The Daily Plant — Indian Grass (Sorghastrum nutans)
item.description:
Sorghastrum nutans, Indian grass, is one of the Big Four tallgrass prairie grasses and one of the most underspecified native warm-season grasses in East Coast design work. This episode covers its genuine East Coast native range, the critical provenance distinction between Midwest and coastal ecotypes, culture requirements (especially the well-drained soil imperative), specific ecological roles including larval host relationships with two skipper species, and a comparison of the three main ornamental cultivars: Sioux Blue, Indian Steel, and Bluebird. Closes with a six-plant spaced-repetition quiz covering Hydrangea, Asclepias, Pycnanthemum, Hibiscus, Agastache, and Coreopsis.

item.title: The Daily Plant — Giant Hyssop and Hummingbird Mint (Agastache)
item.description:
Agastache is one of the most misrepresented genera in the East Coast garden trade — the tag often says native, but the plant in the pot is frequently a desert southwestern hybrid with almost no connection to the eastern plant community. This episode unpacks the full genus: the true eastern natives Agastache nepetoides and Agastache scrophulariifolia, the commonly sold but Midwestern Agastache foeniculum, and the cultivar world anchored by Blue Fortune — with clear guidance on what to specify, what to avoid, and why drainage is the single make-or-break variable for every Agastache on the East Coast.

item.title: The Daily Plant — Tickseeds (Coreopsis and Anacis)

item.title: The Daily Plant — Buttonbush (Cephalanthus occidentalis)
item.description:
Cephalanthus occidentalis — buttonbush — is the definitive native shrub for wet sites on the East Coast, blooming in fragrant spherical white flower clusters from June through September when most shrubs have nothing to offer. This episode covers the plant's culture and the honest limits of its moisture requirement, its exceptional ecological value as a larval host for more than twenty Lepidoptera species and critical habitat for wood ducks, and the cultivar landscape — particularly Sugar Shack, which has made buttonbush genuinely specifiable in designed rain gardens and stormwater plantings at a fraction of the species' scale.
